learning_goal: Name the three hamstrings and their heads, give the common origin from the ischial tuberosity and the two different insertions, state the rule that defines a hamstring and the one head that breaks it, and explain why the tibial and common fibular divisions of the sciatic nerve matter here.

structures.name: long head of right biceps femoris
structures.label: Biceps femoris — long head
structures.narration: The lateral hamstring. It arises with semitendinosus from the ischial tuberosity, crosses both the hip and the knee, and is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. Its tendon is the cord you can feel on the outer side behind a bent knee.

structures.name: short head of right biceps femoris
structures.label: Biceps femoris — short head
structures.narration: The exception that examiners love. It arises from the linea aspera on the femur, not from the ischium, so it crosses only the knee. It is also the one head supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve. On both counts — origin and nerve — it fails the definition of a true hamstring.

structures.name: right semitendinosus
structures.label: Semitendinosus
structures.narration: Named for its tendon, which is half the length of the muscle. It shares a common origin with the long head of biceps femoris and ends on the medial surface of the tibia as part of the pes anserinus. Its cord-like tendon is the more superficial and prominent of the two you feel on the medial side of the back of the knee — semimembranosus is the broader one lying deep to it — and it is commonly harvested as a graft.

structures.name: right semimembranosus
structures.label: Semimembranosus
structures.narration: Named for the flat membranous tendon at its upper end, which lies deep to semitendinosus. It arises from the ischial tuberosity on its own facet, lateral and above the other two, and ends on the back of the medial condyle of the tibia. An expansion of its tendon reinforces the back of the knee capsule, and its bursa is the usual source of a popliteal cyst.

structures.name: right adductor magnus
structures.label: Adductor magnus — hamstring part
structures.narration: A muscle with two halves and two nerves. Its adductor part comes off the pubis and is supplied by the obturator nerve; its posterior part comes off the ischial tuberosity, runs to the adductor tubercle and is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. That posterior part behaves as a fourth hamstring and extends the hip. Give it when a question asks for the hip extensors and expects more than gluteus maximus and the three hamstrings.

structures.name: right gracilis
structures.label: Gracilis
structures.narration: A strap muscle of the medial compartment on the obturator nerve, not a hamstring. It matters here only because it lands on the tibia beside semitendinosus.

structures.name: right sartorius
structures.label: Sartorius
structures.narration: The third tendon of the pes anserinus, and the most anterior of the three. Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus land together on the medial tibia on three different nerves — femoral, obturator and sciatic. One footprint, three nerves; that is the point of learning the goose's foot.

structures.name: right gluteus maximus
structures.label: Gluteus maximus
structures.narration: The upper ends of the hamstrings pass under the lower border of gluteus maximus, so the common origin is not palpable in a standing patient. Both extend the hip, but on different nerves and at different times: the hamstrings do the ordinary walking and gluteus maximus joins in for the heavy work.

structures.name: medial head of right gastrocnemius
structures.label: Gastrocnemius — medial head
structures.narration: The lower medial border of the popliteal fossa. It arises above the knee, from the back of the medial femoral condyle.

structures.name: lateral head of right gastrocnemius
structures.label: Gastrocnemius — lateral head
structures.narration: The lower lateral border of the same diamond. Above it, the tendon of biceps femoris and the common fibular nerve run together towards the neck of the fibula.

structures.name: right hip bone
structures.label: Hip bone
structures.narration: The ischial tuberosity is the whole story of the origin. It is the bone you sit on, it carries two facets — one for semimembranosus, one shared by semitendinosus and the long head of biceps — and it is the site that avulses in a young sprinter.

structures.name: right femur
structures.label: Femur
structures.narration: Only two things in this scene touch the femur: the short head of biceps femoris arising from the linea aspera, and the posterior part of adductor magnus ending at the adductor tubercle. Every other hamstring skips the bone entirely and goes from the pelvis to the leg.

structures.name: right tibia
structures.label: Tibia
structures.narration: The medial landing site. Semitendinosus lands on its medial surface with gracilis and sartorius; semimembranosus lands behind, on the medial condyle.

structures.name: right fibula
structures.label: Fibula
structures.narration: The lateral landing site, and a dangerous one. Both heads of biceps femoris insert into the head of the fibula, and the common fibular nerve winds round the neck just below it, where it lies against bare bone. A fracture or a tight cast there gives foot drop.

structures.label: Adductor tubercle
structures.calibrated_by: geometry: CONTACT, the point where adductor magnus meets the femur (gap 0.49 mm on a 440 mm bone); tools/derive-landmark.mjs --parent FMA24474 --contact FMA22459, unchanged under --slab z:0,0.15. Same measurement as gross__thigh__adductor-canal and gross__thigh__femur, re-derived here rather than copied.
structures.narration: Where the hamstring part of adductor magnus ends, and the reason this muscle counts as half a hamstring: its ischial fibres run to a tendon on this tubercle and are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve, exactly like the true hamstrings beside it.

views.title: The back of the thigh
views.narration: Three muscles fill the posterior compartment of the thigh: biceps femoris on the lateral side, semitendinosus and semimembranosus on the medial side. Biceps femoris has two heads, so there are four bellies but three names. Count them that way and you will not be caught out.

views.title: One origin for nearly all of them
views.narration: The common hamstring origin is the ischial tuberosity. Semimembranosus takes its own facet, above and lateral; semitendinosus and the long head of biceps share a facet below and medial to it. Because the origin is on the pelvis, these muscles cross the hip as well as the knee — which is the definition of a hamstring.

views.title: The head that is not a hamstring
views.narration: Compare the two heads of biceps femoris. The long head starts on the ischium and is tibial; the short head starts on the linea aspera of the femur and is common fibular. So the short head crosses one joint, not two, and it is the only muscle of the compartment on the fibular division. Three things make a true hamstring: an ischial origin, an action at two joints, and a tibial nerve supply. The short head has none of them.

views.title: Two very different endings
views.narration: Below the knee the group splits in two. Biceps femoris goes laterally to the head of the fibula; semitendinosus and semimembranosus go medially to the tibia. Feel the back of your own bent knee — one cord laterally, two medially — and you have identified all three muscles without a single label.

views.title: The goose's foot
views.narration: Three tendons converge on the upper medial tibia: sartorius in front, gracilis in the middle, semitendinosus behind. Together they are the pes anserinus. Learn them in that order from front to back with their nerves — femoral, obturator, sciatic — because that trio of nerves on one insertion is a favourite question.

views.title: What they do
views.narration: They flex the knee and extend the hip. Because most of them cross both joints they cannot shorten fully at both at once: with the hip flexed the knee cannot be fully extended, which is exactly what a straight leg raise tests. In walking, they are the muscles that decelerate the swinging leg before the heel strikes — they work most just before the foot lands, not when it pushes off.

views.title: They rotate the flexed knee
views.narration: With the knee bent, the lateral one turns the leg outwards and the medial two turn it inwards. That is simply their line of pull: biceps femoris passes to the lateral side, the other two to the medial side. Rotation is only possible in flexion — the extended knee is locked.

views.title: One nerve, two divisions
views.narration: The path traced here is the sciatic nerve. It enters the back of the thigh below gluteus maximus, lies on adductor magnus, and supplies the whole compartment as it descends. Its tibial division supplies all the hamstrings except one; its common fibular division supplies only the short head of biceps femoris and then runs on to the neck of the fibula. The sciatic nerve's own root value is L4 to S3; the hamstrings themselves draw mainly on L5, S1 and S2.

views.title: A cut across the back of the thigh
views.narration: Slide the cut down the thigh. Biceps femoris sits laterally, semitendinosus superficial and medial with semimembranosus flat beneath it, and adductor magnus forms the floor with the sciatic nerve lying on it. The posterior compartment is separated from the anterior one by the intermuscular septa running from the fascia lata to the linea aspera.

views.title: The diamond behind the knee
views.narration: As the three muscles separate above the knee they open a diamond. Biceps femoris makes the upper lateral border, semitendinosus and semimembranosus the upper medial border, and the two heads of gastrocnemius the lower two. That diamond is the popliteal fossa, and it is where you feel the popliteal pulse — deepest of all the structures in it, against the bone.

views.title: Why hamstrings tear
views.narration: A two-joint muscle lengthening under load is the muscle that tears. It happens at the end of the swing phase in sprinting, when the hip is flexed and the knee is straightening and the hamstrings are braking both. The long head of biceps femoris tears most often, near the junction of muscle and tendon. In an adolescent the tendon holds and the ischial tuberosity apophysis pulls off instead, because the growth plate is the weakest link before it fuses.

views.title: Peel the back of the thigh
views.narration: The dissection order to recite: skin and fascia lata, then the lower border of gluteus maximus, then the sciatic nerve entering the compartment, then semitendinosus and biceps femoris superficially, then semimembranosus, then adductor magnus as the floor, then the femur. Four layers, and every structure in the posterior thigh has an address.

gaps: No nerve of the lower limb exists as a model. The sciatic nerve — the single most important structure in this compartment — is authored as a traced concept path down the muscles it supplies, and the split into tibial and common fibular divisions is narration only. The common fibular nerve winding round the neck of the fibula is taught by lighting the fibula and naming it.

There is no popliteal artery or vein in the catalog, so the contents of the popliteal fossa are described rather than shown. The fossa itself is the separate Popliteal fossa curriculum entry, which this scene does not claim to cover.

No tendon is modelled separately from its muscle, so the long cord of semitendinosus, the membranous upper tendon of semimembranosus and the conjoint tendon of the common origin are taught from the muscle bellies and the narration.

The ischial tuberosity, the linea aspera and the head of the fibula are sub-features of whole-bone meshes, taught by lighting the hip bone, femur or fibula and naming the feature. The adductor tubercle is no longer on that list: it is measurable as the contact between adductor magnus and the femur (0.49 mm) and is now a measured anchor in this scene. The other three are ridges or broad areas rather than points and have not yet been given a definition the landmark tool can measure.
The sacrotuberous ligament, which the common hamstring origin blends with, has no mesh in the catalog and is described in narration.
The semimembranosus bursa is not modelled, so a popliteal cyst is mentioned rather than shown.

The fascia lata and the intermuscular septa that close the posterior compartment have no mesh — searched as fascia, fasciae latae, tract and septum, and the only fascial models in the catalog are the iliotibial tract and tensor fasciae latae, neither of which is the compartment boundary this scene needs. Beat 9 therefore names the septa running from the fascia lata to the linea aspera without drawing them.

This scene does not cover Femur, Gluteus maximus, Sciatic nerve or Popliteal fossa. Gluteus maximus appears only as the muscle whose lower border the hamstrings pass under, the gastrocnemius heads only as the lower borders of the diamond, and the bones only as the frame.
